Learning Objectives
Understand that constant attention to infection prevention best practices is intrinsic to
modern orthopaedic surgical practice.
Review the importance of preoperative patient selection, risk assessment, and optimization in
infection prevention.
Explain why optimal perioperative practices, including alcohol-based skin preparation,
adequate but not excessive peri-incisional antibiotic prophylaxis, and hand hygiene, make
surgery safer with lower infection rates.

Background
Perioperative safety is critical to successful orthopaedic practice.
Perioperative infections often can be avoided via adequate safety measures, patient selection,
and perioperative optimization.

Background
Modern orthopaedic techniques improve the lives of hundreds of millions of individuals
around the world each year. Postoperative infections are common; for example, 1% to
2% of all patients who undergo hip or knee arthroplasty sustain an infection within 2
years postoperatively. These infections are costly and may be devastating for patients
and their families. Strategies to prevent infections are critical.
Preoperative Patient Selection
Risk factors for infection are divided into those that are modifiable and those that are
nonmodifiable.1 Optimizing modifiable risk factors and considering the risk-to-benefit ratio in
the context of the overall risk factor profile are critical before elective orthopaedic surgery.
Risk factors for postoperative orthopaedic surgical site infections (SSIs) are best described in
arthroplasty and spine surgery.

Preoperative Patient Selection
A number of studies indicate that patients who are more sick have poorer outcomes and
more frequent infections after orthopaedic surgery regardless whether the illness is an
autoimmune, metabolic, neoplastic, psychiatric, or other disorder. Most of these studies
are retrospective in nature, and large prospective cohort studies are rare.
Modifiable Risk Factors

Other infections
COVID-19

Immunosuppressive states
HIV/AIDS
Rheumatoid arthritis in patients being treated with biologic agents or steroids
Obesity and malnutrition
Staphylococcus aureus colonization
Recent corticosteroid injection in patients undergoing hip or knee arthroplasty
Dental disease
Tobacco, alcohol, and illicit drug use

Modifiable Risk Factors
The causative organisms of most orthopaedic surgical infections are the same as those
of most skin and soft-tissue infections or are skin commensals, including S aureus,
coagulase-negative staphylococci, streptococci, enterococci, and Cutibacterium acnes.
Postponing elective orthopaedic surgery in patients with an active skin infection may
decrease the rate of SSI via direct communication with the wound. In addition, remote
infections may increase the risk of bacteremia, particularly if implants are being used.
Optimally, elective orthopaedic surgery should be performed in patients without
evidence of an active bacterial infection.2,3
Dermatoses, such as psoriasis and eczema, and deficits in skin integrity, such as diabetic
and vascular ulcers, may be associated with an increased risk of infection after elective
orthopaedic surgery.4,5 Eczematous skin is colonized with S aureus in approximately
70% of patients.6 Elective orthopaedic surgery should be deferred until open wounds
have healed and closed, and incisions should not be made in areas of active dermatosis.

Dermatophytosis of the lower extremities and skin folds is very common; however, the
fungal organisms that cause dermatophytosis are extremely rare as pathogens in
patients with an orthopaedic infection.7 Instead, the presence of diseased skin may
increase the risk of surgical infection by facilitating the transcutaneous translocation of
bacteria. Dermatophytosis may be simple to manage via a brief course of topical
antifungal agents or may be recalcitrant and even an indicator of underlying illness (eg,
recurrent severe tinea cruris and uncontrolled diabetes mellitus).
Routine universal preoperative urinary screening was routine in many orthopaedic
centers; however, this practice largely has decreased. Although asymptomatic
bacteriuria is common, particularly in older women, management via antibiotic agents is
not indicated in asymptomatic patients during routine primary care or in the
perioperative setting. In patients with signs and symptoms of a urinary tract infection,
treatment should be prioritized and surgical treatment should be postponed if feasible
because risks of infection may increase.8
In patients with an acute infection, elective orthopaedic surgery can be reasonably
postponed until the infection has resolved and the patient is optimized for surgery.
The effects of the COVID-19 pandemic remain substantial worldwide. Performing
orthopaedic surgery in patients with an active COVID-19 infection is associated with high
mortality and morbidity rates. Large cohort studies indicate that active or recent COVID-
19 infection increases the risk of mortality and severe postoperative complications;9,10
therefore, elective surgery should be postponed. Recovery from COVID-19 infection may
lead to resolution of this risk.11 Future studies are needed to determine the effects of
COVID-19 infection on downstream orthopaedic outcomes.
Diabetes mellitus is common in orthopaedic populations. Although studies have not
universally reported an association between diabetes mellitus and poorer outcomes,
most studies and metanalyses indicate poorer outcomes in patients with diabetes
mellitus (chronic) and patients with hyperglycemia (acute) who undergo orthopaedic
surgery.12,13

Mechanisms by which diabetes mellitus increases the risk of poorer outcomes include
the sequelae of chronic hyperglycemia, including peripheral microvascular and
neurologic disease, and the presence of perioperative hyperglycemia, which has direct
effects on wound healing and immune function. Hyperglycemia is an important risk
factor independent of diabetes mellitus. Hyperglycemia increases the risk of SSI of the
spine in patients without a diabetic spine and in trauma patients.14,15
Elevated hemoglobin A1c levels (a measure of glycemia over approximately 3 months), in
fructosamine levels (indicative of glycemia over 2 to 3 weeks), and serum glucose levels
at the point of care are associated with an increased risk of postoperative complications,
including infection.16
Perioperative treatment for people with diabetes mellitus is best provided in a
multidisciplinary framework involving structured order sets, experienced clinicians, and
attention to diet. Although intensive glycemic control has not been found to improve
perioperative outcomes in orthopaedics, a target of 180 mg/dL may be used for the
initiation of insulin therapy in hyperglycemic patients postoperatively. 16
Hemoglobin A1c thresholds, above which the risk of adverse events is substantially
increased, appear to exist in some but not all orthopaedic studies in various populations.
In general, hemoglobin A1c levels between 7% and 8% appear to confer a substantially
increased risk of adverse events,17-19 such that many medical centers postpone surgery
in patients with a hemoglobin A1c level above this threshold until their diabetes mellitus
is better controlled.
Advances in medical science, including in transplant medicine, cancer chemotherapy,
and the management of inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, have prolonged and
improved the lives of millions of individuals each year at the expense of immune
protection. Performing orthopaedic surgery in an immunocompromised patient is
associated with an increased risk of infection; however, prospective data often are
lacking.

HIV/AIDS appears to confer an increased risk of prosthetic joint infection after elective
arthroplasty; however, compliance with antiretroviral medications modulates this risk.20-
22 In patients with HIV, elective surgery optimally should be performed in those with an
undetectable viral load and in whom a cluster of differentiation 4 count has been
optimized.
Patients with rheumatoid arthritis or a related inflammatory disorder constitute an
important orthopaedic subgroup with an increased risk of postoperative infection. This
increased risk likely is the result of a combination of factors, including dysregulated
immunity; increased prevalence of staphylococcal nasal and skin carriage; and
immunomodulatory treatments, particularly corticosteroids and biologic agents.
Perioperative co-management with attention to proper immunomodulatory medication
management may improve outcomes.23
Obesity is prevalent in the United States and is recognized as a risk factor for poor
medical outcomes and increased mortality.24 Most studies have found associations
between obesity and an increased risk for infection in patients who undergo arthroplasty
or spine surgery.25, 26-28 Although debate exists with regard to a threshold body mass
index above which elective surgery may be excessively risky, a body mass index greater
than 40 kg/m2 is considered a threshold for elective surgery at many medical centers.
Among individuals with obesity, weight loss, whether via diet and exercise,
pharmacotherapy, or bariatric surgery, is associated with improved general health
status; however, weight loss in patients with obesity may not improve orthopaedic
outcomes, including the risk of postoperative infection.29, 30 The role of malnutrition
with regard to an increased risk of infection is more difficult to determine; however,
imperfect indicators, such as serum albumin level and total lymphocyte count, have
been associated with infection risk in patients who undergo arthroplasty.31, 32
Glucocorticoids inhibit multiple types of immune cells and alter infection risk and wound
healing. Chronic glucocorticoid use appears to increase the risk of periprosthetic joint
infection;28, 33 therefore, doses in the preoperative period should be tapered to the
minimum required. Various studies indicate that intra-articular injections increase the

risk of periprosthetic joint infection in a time-dependent fashion. 34, 35 A similar
association has been observed between instrumented and non-instrumented spine
surgery infections and epidural corticosteroid injections.36, 37
Active dentogingival infection is a contraindication to elective orthopaedic surgery,
particularly if implants are being used. Older adults, particularly those with medical
comorbidities, may have an increased risk for dental pathology. Recommendations on
the need for dental clearance before total joint arthroplasty differ.38-40 Dental clearance
may not be an absolute prerequisite for orthopaedic surgery in asymptomatic
candidates; however, screening for risk factors and active symptoms is recommended if
orthopaedic implants are anticipated.
The role of antibiotic prophylaxis in patients with a total joint arthroplasty implant who
are undergoing dental care has been a subject of great debate for decades, and
antibiotic prophylaxis varies widely between and within countries. The American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Appropriate Use Criteria on the Management of
Patients with Orthopaedic Implants Undergoing Dental Procedures suggest that dental
prophylaxis may be offered to patients in certain higher risk groups;41 however, recent
studies continue to suggest that invasive dental procedures do not increase the risk of
periprosthetic joint infection and that antibiotic prophylaxis is not beneficial.42
Current, but not historical, tobacco use increases the risk of orthopaedic infections in
patients undergoing total joint arthroplasty and spine surgery.43, 44 High alcohol
consumption and parenteral drug use are increase the risk for infection and poor
outcomes in patients with various health states, including those undergoing arthroplasty
surgery.43 Orthopaedic complications are prevalent in patients who use intravenous
drugs given the high rate of bacteremia; therefore, elective surgery that involves the use
of large implants is contraindicated in patients who use drugs until they have been
treated adequately and the likelihood of relapse is low.45, 46
Nonmodifiable Risk Factors

S aureus Decolonization
Methicillin-susceptible S aureus and methicillin-resistant S aureus are leading causes of
orthopaedic infections and are present in to 30% to 40% and 2% to 4% of humans,
respectively.47, 48
Although targeted or universal decolonization strategies are implemented to varying extents in
hospitals around the country, studies have not reached a consensus on whether standard
decolonization is substantially effective in patients undergoing orthopaedic surgery.

S aureus Decolonization
Multiple studies have shown that S aureus nasal colonization increases the risk of SSI.
Emerging data from observational and smaller trials have shown some benefit to
decolonization; however, the risk of infection remains in previously decolonized
individuals.49-51
Multiple strategies to reduce the risk of infection in general and specific patient groups
are under evaluation. These include universal decolonization, in which all surgical
candidates undergo decolonization preoperatively, usually via a combination of
mupirocin and chlorhexidine for 5 days, and targeted decolonization strategies, in which
decolonization regimens are offered to patients with evidence for or an increased risk of
colonization. Povidone-iodine-based decolonization may be simpler for patients and
similarly effective.52 Such strategies may be laboratory-based (culture or polymerase
chain reaction), based on a history of infection, or based on comorbid risks
(hospitalization in the past year, residence in a long-term care facility, or
immunocompromised).
Beyond mupirocin and chlorhexidine, decolonization regimens used in some centers
include iodine- or alcohol-containing products and other less commonly used topical

Infection Prevention
Healthcare Workers: Routine and Universal Precautions
Routine hand hygiene
Performed before and after every clinical encounter by all staff members working in the
clinical space with the use of alcohol-based hand sanitizer or soap and water.
Because hand hygiene compliance is better with alcohol-based hand sanitizer, it is
recommended for routine use by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
Routine hand hygiene also must be performed at other key moments during care (eg, before
moving from a dirty task to a clean task, such as after the removal of a used dressing and the
placement of a new one, every time gloves are removed [even if putting on a new pair], and
after contact with a possibly contaminated object or surface).
Surgical hand hygiene
Removing debris from under fingernails followed by adequate cleaning of hands with the use
of a product that has persistent activity (ie, an antimicrobial soap or an alcohol-based
surgical hand sanitizer) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions are critical before
gowning and gloving to eliminate transient hand flora and reduce resident hand flora that
may be released into the surgical field if gloves become punctured or torn during surgery.
After caring for a patient with known or suspected sporicidal pathogens (most importantly,
Clostridioides difficile), which are partially resistant to hand sanitizers and require mechanical
removal with the use of soap and running water
After caring for a patient with known or suspected infectious diarrhea
If hands are visibly soiled

Healthcare Workers: Routine and Universal Precautions
Hand hygiene, from the earliest days of healthcare infection prevention with
Semmelweis, remains critical (Resources 1, 2, and 3). The surgical scrub, the process of
cleaning hands before gloving and gowning, reduces bacterial load but does not sterilize
a surgeon’s hands. Adherence to safe practices in all clinical interactions in the hospital

and clinic, including the proper use of alcohol-based hand sanitizers or soap and water
to perform effective hand hygiene, also is important.
Situations may occur in which hand hygiene must be performed with the use of soap
and water rather than an alcohol-based product.
In routine hospital use, the CDC recommends standard use of 60% or higher alcohol-
based products because of their convenience and higher compliance among healthcare
workers.
Surgical hand antisepsis should include close attention to cleaning under the fingernails,
and the hands and forearms, generally for 2 to 6 minutes, without general need for
longer scrub times. Double gloving is advised during invasive procedures associated with
an increased risk of exposure to blood and other fluids.
Patient Interventions
Body cleansing
Preoperative body cleansing with the use of standard or antiseptic soaps before orthopaedic
surgery is a common practice; however, strong data demonstrating a reduction in SSI are
lacking.
Body hair removal
Although body hair removal is common before orthopaedic surgery, the literature examining
the practice has not clearly noted its benefit.
Avoid shaving; instead, perioperative clipping or depilatory creams are recommended.

Patient Interventions
Universal preoperative body cleansing with the use of standard or antiseptic soaps has
become standard in many orthopaedic practices. The efficacy of universal preoperative
body cleansing remains unclear, and the additional benefit of the use of antiseptic
agents, such as chlorhexidine gluconate, over regular soap remains unproven. Although

some observational studies have suggested reductions in SSI rates,53, 54 no rigorous
studies have shown statistically meaningful advantages. Although US guidelines, such as
those of the Institute for Healthcare Improvement, favor the use of chlorhexidine
bathing before arthroplasty, most international organizations do not.
The removal of body hair is only indicated if the presence of hair may interfere with
surgery or wound healing.55 Hair removal should be performed before incision, not the
night before surgery. Shaving should be avoided because it may lead to increased
infection rates, presumably from enhanced pathogen adhesion to denuded and injured
skin. Instead, depilatory agents and hair clipping are recommended.56
Surgical Skin Preparation
Alcohol-based antiseptic products containing chlorhexidine or iodine are superior to and
should be used instead of non–alcohol-based products to reduce the risk of SSI.

Surgical Skin Preparation
Contraindications are uncommon in orthopaedic surgery but may include skin reactions
or exposure of mucous membranes to the antiseptic product.
Surgeons should be aware of the uncommon risk of operating room fires if alcohol-
based products pool and/or are not allowed to dry long enough per manufacturer
guidance and are exposed to adequate heat and oxygen.58
Manufacturer instructions for application technique and time and drying time must be
followed to ensure patient safety, staff safety, and surgical skin preparation
effectiveness. (Video 1)

Antibiotic Prophylaxis
Perioperative Antibiotic Agents
A single dose of an antibiotic agent, typically cefazolin, is indicated before incision, during
orthopaedic procedures including spinal surgery, and during the implantation of orthopaedic
hardware (including fixation and arthroplasty).
Antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated (but is frequently used in practice) in clean procedures
involving the hand, knee, or foot with no implantation of foreign material.
Antibiotic agents should be re-dosed during lengthy surgical procedures; however, the
continuation of prophylactic antibiotic agents should not exceed closure of the incision or
extend more than 24 hours for any indication.
Adherence to national guidelines59 for perioperative prophylaxis and avoidance of overly
broad coverage and excessively long duration are preferred to decrease selection pressure for

multidrug-resistant organisms, to decrease the risk of adverse drug reactions, and to minimize
the rate of C difficile.

Perioperative Antibiotic Agents
The development of antibiotic agents was soon followed by the finding that short
courses of antibiotic agents administered within the immediate peri-incisional period
lowered infection rates. This finding has led to drastic improvements in SSI rates in
multiple surgical subspecialties.
Surgical wounds frequently become contaminated by a patient’s own skin flora by the
end of the procedure; this colonization is dependent on the duration of the surgical
procedure. Effective perioperative antibiotic agents decrease SSI rates by reaching
bactericidal levels and preventing contaminating skin flora from surviving long enough to
initiate infection.
Current national guidelines recommend weight-based cefazolin as a standard antibiotic
agent for patients without substantial allergies to beta-lactams. In patients with
substantial allergy, acceptable alternatives in orthopaedic surgery include vancomycin
and clindamycin.59
To achieve adequate bactericidal concentrations throughout lengthier procedures,
intraoperative redosing guidelines favor redosing after two pharmacokinetic half-lives:
cefazolin should be re-dosed after 6 hours in most patients undergoing lengthy surgical
procedures.
CDC guidelines for clean and clean-contaminated surgeries recommend that
prophylactic antibiotic agents not be administered after wound closure, even in patients
with a drain, and that no topical antibiotic agents be administered to the wound bed.
Despite CDC recommendations that no perioperative antibiotic agents be administered
on incision closure, variability in the duration of prophylaxis exists in orthopaedics.
Completion of a 24-hour course of cefazolin is common, and a recent influential but

suboptimally controlled study60, 61 has prompted even longer courses of antibiotic
agents in high-risk patients undergoing arthroplasty. No randomized study has directly
compared single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis with 24-hour antibiotic prophylaxis (or any
duration longer than 24 hours) in orthopaedic surgery; available data suggest
equivalence.62 No randomized data suggest that prolonging prophylaxis beyond the first
postoperative day (or beyond wound closure) offers any clinical advantage.
Finally, evidence suggests that vancomycin powder applied to surgical wounds may
decrease the risk of infection. In a study on high-risk tibial articular fractures, an
infection was considerably less likely to develop in an arm with vancomycin compared
with a control arm (6.4% versus 9.8%).63A meta-analysis of studies on the use of
vancomycin in spine surgery suggested a benefit (odds ratio, 0.39);64 however, of the
three randomized studies included in the meta-analysis, none suggested a benefit.
Additional Further randomized studies in other surgical patient groups are necessary to
evaluate the advantages and risks of intrawound vancomycin powder.
